lessons.title: Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
lessons.body: When you pick up a piece of metal in the workshop, the first thing to know is whether it contains iron. If it does, it's ferrous. If it doesn't, it's non-ferrous. This matters because ferrous metals rust when exposed to moisture, while most non-ferrous metals do not. You can test with a magnet: ferrous metals are magnetic (with a few exceptions like stainless steel), non-ferrous are not. In Africa, common ferrous metals include mild steel, which you'll find in car bodies, roofing sheets, and gates. It's strong and cheap but rusts fast. Non-ferrous metals include aluminum, copper, brass, and zinc. Aluminum is light and resists corrosion, often used for cooking pots, window frames, and roofing. Copper is used for electrical wiring and roofing because it conducts electricity and weathers to a green patina. Brass, a mix of copper and zinc, is used for decorative items and fittings. Knowing the difference helps you choose the right metal for the job. For example, in coastal areas like Mombasa or Lagos, salt in the air speeds up rust, so you'd avoid mild steel outdoors unless it's well painted or galvanized. In dry regions like the Sahel, mild steel lasts longer. Also, when you weld or cut, ferrous metals give off sparks that are long and straight, while non-ferrous sparks are short and few. This quick test can save you from mixing metals incorrectly. Always keep ferrous and non-ferrous scrap separate at your workplace; mixing them can ruin a batch when recycling. Remember: ferrous equals iron, rust, and magnetic; non-ferrous equals no iron, no rust, and non-magnetic. That simple rule will guide your material choices every day.

lessons.title: Common Sheet Metal Alloys: Steel, Aluminum, Copper
lessons.body: Alloys are metals mixed with other elements to improve their properties. In sheet metal work, you'll mostly use three: steel, aluminum, and copper. Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. Mild steel (also called low-carbon steel) has about 0.05% to 0.25% carbon. It's strong, easy to weld, and cheap. You'll see it in car panels, filing cabinets, and roofing sheets. But it rusts, so it's often galvanized (coated with zinc) or painted. Stainless steel has chromium (at least 10.5%) which forms a protective layer, making it rust-resistant. It's used for kitchen sinks, cutlery, and medical equipment. It's harder to cut and weld, and more expensive. Aluminum is not an alloy by itself, but it's often alloyed with copper, manganese, or silicon to make it stronger. Pure aluminum is soft and ductile, great for shaping. Alloyed aluminum (like 6061) is used for aircraft, bicycles, and window frames. It's about one-third the weight of steel, resists corrosion, and conducts heat well, so it's ideal for cooking pots. However, it's softer and can dent easily. Copper is a pure metal, but it's also used in alloys like brass (copper + zinc) and bronze (copper + tin). Copper sheet is used for roofing, gutters, and decorative work. It's expensive but lasts over 100 years and develops a green patina. It's very malleable and conducts electricity, so it's also used in electrical components. In Africa, you'll find steel widely available and affordable. Aluminum is common in urban areas for roofing and utensils. Copper is less common but prized for art and roofing in historic buildings. When choosing, consider cost, strength, corrosion resistance, and workability. For a simple water trough in a rural area, galvanized steel is best. For a lightweight roof in a coastal city, aluminum wins. For a decorative sign, copper or brass gives a premium look. Always check the alloy number if buying new stock; it tells you its properties.

lessons.title: Material Properties: Ductility, Malleability, Hardness
lessons.body: To work sheet metal well, you need to understand three key properties: ductility, malleability, and hardness. Ductility is the ability of a metal to be stretched into a wire without breaking. Think of copper wireâit can be pulled thin and still conduct electricity. In sheet metal, ductility allows you to bend a sheet around a tight radius without cracking. For example, aluminum is very ductile, so you can hammer it into shapes. Mild steel is also ductile, but less than aluminum. Malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. It's similar to ductility but involves compression rather than tension. Gold is the most malleable metal, but in your workshop, copper and aluminum are highly malleable. You can hammer copper into bowls or roof flashing. Hardness is the resistance to scratching, cutting, or indentation. Hard metals like stainless steel are difficult to scratch but also hard to cut and form. Soft metals like aluminum scratch easily but are easy to work. You can test hardness with a file: a file bites into soft metal but slides on hard metal. Or use a center punch and hammer: a deep mark means soft. These properties affect your tools and methods. For ductile and malleable metals, you can use hand shears, hammers, and English wheels. For hard metals, you need power shears, angle grinders, and maybe annealing (heating and cooling) to soften them. Annealing copper: heat it to cherry red and quench in waterâit becomes soft again. Annealing steel: heat and cool slowly. In Africa, many workshops use recycled materials, so properties vary. A car panel might be mild steel, easy to shape. A cooking pot might be aluminum, easy to dent but also easy to hammer back. Always test a small piece before starting a big job. Remember: ductility for bending, malleability for hammering, hardness for wear resistance. Balance them for the task.

lessons.title: Gauge System and Thickness Measurement
lessons.body: Sheet metal thickness is measured by gauge, a number that tells you how thick the metal is. The higher the gauge number, the thinner the metal. For example, 16 gauge is thicker than 20 gauge. But be careful: gauge numbers differ for ferrous and non-ferrous metals. For steel, a common standard is the Standard Wire Gauge (SWG) or the American Wire Gauge (AWG). In many African countries, SWG is used. For aluminum, the Brown & Sharpe gauge is common. To avoid confusion, always ask for thickness in millimeters (mm) or inches. A 20 gauge steel sheet is about 0.9 mm thick, while 20 gauge aluminum is about 0.8 mm. In practice, you'll often work with 0.5 mm to 2 mm sheets. For roofing, 0.5 mm (about 26 gauge) is typical. For car bodies, 0.8 mm to 1.2 mm (20 to 18 gauge) is common. For heavy-duty boxes, 2 mm (14 gauge) or thicker. To measure thickness, use a micrometer or a vernier caliper. A micrometer is more precise, measuring to 0.01 mm. A caliper is cheaper and good enough for most jobs. If you don't have either, you can use a gauge wheel or a simple ruler for rough estimates, but that's not accurate. Another method: compare with known samples. Keep a set of labeled offcuts of different gauges. When you get new stock, compare its stiffness and weight. Thicker sheets are harder to bend by hand; you'll need a bending brake. Thinner sheets can be cut with hand shears. Also, when ordering, specify the gauge and the standard (e.g.,

). In Africa, suppliers may use different standards, so always verify with a caliper. Buying the wrong gauge can ruin a job: too thin and it dents easily; too thick and you can't form it. For most general work, 20 gauge (0.9 mm) is a good all-round thickness. Keep a conversion chart on your wall: 10 gauge = 3.2 mm, 16 gauge = 1.6 mm, 20 gauge = 0.9 mm, 24 gauge = 0.6 mm. That will save you time and mistakes.

lessons.title: Corrosion and Material Protection
lessons.body: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of metal by chemical reaction with its environment. For ferrous metals, rust is the main enemy. Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. In Africa, humidity, salt air along the coast, and acid rain in industrial areas speed up corrosion. Non-ferrous metals like aluminum and copper also corrode, but the products are usually protective. Aluminum forms a thin oxide layer that stops further corrosion. Copper forms a green patina that protects it. But steel rusts away. To protect steel, you have several methods. Painting is the cheapest: clean the metal, apply a primer, then a topcoat. For outdoor use, use epoxy or polyurethane paint. Galvanizing is coating steel with zinc. It's done by hot-dip galvanizing (dipping in molten zinc) or electroplating. Galvanized sheets are common for roofing and buckets. The zinc sacrifices itself to protect the steel. You can also use zinc-rich paint. Another method is powder coating: electrically charged powder baked onto the metal. It's tough and comes in many colors. For small parts, you can oil or grease them, but that attracts dust. In rural areas, used motor oil is a common rust preventative for tools. For aluminum, anodizing thickens the oxide layer for better corrosion resistance and allows dyeing. For copper, a clear lacquer can preserve the shine, but many prefer the patina. When joining different metals, beware of galvanic corrosion. If you bolt aluminum to steel in a wet environment, the aluminum will corrode faster. Use insulating washers or a barrier like paint. Also, avoid scratching galvanized surfaces; the zinc coating is sacrificial but a deep scratch exposes steel. In your workshop, keep metal dry, stack sheets with spacers for air circulation, and apply a protective coat as soon as possible after fabrication. Remember: corrosion never sleeps, but with the right protection, your work can last for decades.

lessons.title: Material Selection for Specific Applications
lessons.body: Choosing the right sheet metal for a job is critical. You must consider strength, corrosion resistance, weight, cost, and workability. Start by asking: where will it be used? Indoors or outdoors? Coastal or inland? Will it be exposed to chemicals? For roofing in a rainy area, galvanized steel or aluminum are good. Galvanized steel is cheaper but heavier; aluminum is lighter and rust-proof but more expensive and dents easily. For a coastal area, aluminum or stainless steel are better because salt destroys galvanized steel quickly. For a cooking pot, aluminum is ideal: it conducts heat well, is lightweight, and doesn't rust. But it reacts with acidic foods, so avoid cooking tomatoes for long in bare aluminum. Stainless steel is better for acidic foods but costs more and is heavier. For a car body, mild steel is standard because it's strong, easy to form, and cheap. It must be painted to prevent rust. For a decorative sign, copper or brass gives a premium look and weathers beautifully. For a water tank, galvanized steel or plastic-lined steel is common. For a gutter, aluminum or PVC is better than steel because it won't rust. For a heat shield, aluminum or stainless steel reflects heat. For a toolbox, mild steel is fine if painted. For a medical cabinet, stainless steel is required for hygiene. In Africa, availability matters. In many markets, you'll find mild steel, galvanized steel, and aluminum easily. Copper and stainless steel may be limited and expensive. Consider recycled materials: old car panels are mild steel; old roofing sheets are galvanized; old pots are aluminum. But test them for thickness and corrosion. Also, think about joining methods: steel can be welded, aluminum needs TIG or rivets, copper can be soldered. If you lack welding equipment, choose a metal you can bolt or rivet. Finally, consider the environment: termites don't eat metal, but humidity does. For a chicken coop in a humid area, use galvanized steel mesh. For a dry area, mild steel is fine. Always make a sample and test it if possible. A little planning saves a lot of rework.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sheet Metal Materials and Properties

In an African sheet metal workshopâwhether you are fabricating roofing sheets in Kumasi, gutters and fascia in Nairobi, or stainless steel kitchen equipment in Lagosâprofitability depends on matching the right material to the job. This practical reference consolidates the core knowledge from this module into a working tool you can keep at the bench. It covers ferrous and non-ferrous metals, common alloys, key mechanical properties, gauge systems, corrosion protection, and material selection for specific applications, with a business-first focus on reducing waste, avoiding rework, and winning repeat clients.

Sheet metal work is a high-volume, low-margin trade in most African markets. A single wrong gauge choice on a 500-sheet roofing order can wipe out your profit. Understanding material properties is not academicâit is the difference between a business that grows and one that constantly replaces rejected work.

Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals

Ferrous metals contain iron as their base element. They are strong, hard, and relatively cheap, but most are prone to rust unless protected. Common ferrous sheet metals include mild steel (the workhorse of roofing, ducting, and general fabrication), galvanised steel (mild steel coated with zinc), and stainless steel (an alloy of iron, chromium, and often nickel). Stainless steel resists corrosion because chromium forms a passive oxide layer.

Non-ferrous metals contain no iron (or only trace amounts). They are generally lighter, more corrosion-resistant, and more expensive. In African sheet metal work, the most common non-ferrous sheets are aluminium (roofing, cladding, vehicle panels), copper (roofing, gutters, decorative work), and zinc (roofing, flashing). Brass and bronze sheets are used for decorative and marine applications but are less common in general fabrication.

For a business, the choice between ferrous and non-ferrous often comes down to cost versus longevity. Mild steel is affordable but needs painting or galvanising. Aluminium costs more upfront but lasts longer in coastal or humid environments. Copper is the most expensive but can last over a century and command premium prices in high-end construction.

Common Sheet Metal Alloys: Steel, Aluminum, Copper

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. In sheet form, the most common types are:

  • Mild steel (low carbon): Easy to weld, cut, and form. Used for roofing, ducting, and general fabrication. Prone to rust.
  • Galvanised steel: Mild steel dipped in molten zinc or electroplated. The zinc sacrifices itself to protect the steel. Standard for African roofing sheets.
  • Stainless steel (304, 316): Chromium content (typically 18%) provides corrosion resistance. Type 316 adds molybdenum for marine and chemical environments. Used for kitchen equipment, food processing, and coastal applications.

Aluminum is lightweight (about one-third the density of steel), naturally corrosion-resistant (it forms a protective oxide layer), and highly malleable. Common sheet alloys include 1100 (pure aluminium, excellent formability), 3003 (manganese alloy, good corrosion resistance), and 5052 (magnesium alloy, high strength, used in marine and transport). Aluminium cannot be welded with standard steel equipmentâit requires TIG or MIG with aluminium-specific filler.

Copper is highly ductile, thermally and electrically conductive, and naturally corrosion-resistant (it develops a green patina over time). It is used for roofing, gutters, downspouts, and decorative work. Copper is soft and scratches easily, so it requires careful handling. It is also one of the most expensive common sheet metals, making it a premium product for high-end clients.

Material Properties: Ductility, Malleability, Hardness

These three properties determine how a sheet behaves under the hammer, brake, and roller.

Table 1: Key mechanical properties of common sheet metals
Material Ductility Malleability Hardness Forming Notes
Mild Steel High High Medium Easy to bend, weld, and cut. Watch for work hardening.
Galvanised Steel High High Medium Zinc coating can crack if bent sharply; use larger bend radii.
Stainless Steel Medium Medium High Work hardens rapidly; use slow speeds and sharp tooling.
Aluminium High Very High Low Soft and gummy; use lubricant when cutting and drilling.
Copper Very High Very High Low Excellent for hand forming; scratches easily.

Source: ASM International, ASM Metals Handbook, Volume 1, 1990; and Budinski, K.G. & Budinski, M.K., Engineering Materials: Properties and Selection, 9th ed., Pearson, 2010.

Ductility is the ability of a metal to be stretched or drawn without breaking. High-ductility metals can be bent, rolled, or deep-drawn into complex shapes. Aluminium and copper are highly ductile; stainless steel is less so and work hardens quickly.

Malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. It is closely related to ductility but specifically refers to compressive deformation. Copper and aluminium are very malleable; mild steel is moderately malleable; cast iron (not sheet) is not malleable at all.

Hardness is resistance to scratching, abrasion, or indentation. Harder metals resist wear but are more difficult to form and cut. Stainless steel is hard and abrasive; aluminium and copper are soft and prone to scratching. For a business, hardness affects tool wear and cutting speedâstainless steel will dull blades faster than aluminium.

Gauge System and Thickness Measurement

Sheet metal thickness is commonly specified by gauge number. Confusingly, the gauge system is not universal: ferrous and non-ferrous metals use different scales, and the relationship between gauge and thickness is inverseâhigher gauge numbers mean thinner sheets.

Table 2: Approximate sheet metal thickness by gauge (mm)
Gauge Mild Steel (mm) Galvanised Steel (mm) Aluminium (mm) Copper (mm)
84.184.274.194.19
103.423.513.403.40
122.782.752.642.64
141.992.031.631.63
161.521.591.291.29
181.211.271.021.02
200.910.950.810.81
220.760.790.640.64
240.610.640.510.51
260.460.480.400.40

Source: ASTM A480/A480M-22, Standard Specification for General Requirements for Flat-Rolled Stainless and Heat-Resisting Steel Plate, Sheet, and Strip; and ASTM B209-14, Standard Specification for Aluminum and Aluminum-Alloy Sheet and Plate.

In practice, always verify thickness with a micrometer or digital caliper. Gauge labels can be inaccurate, especially on imported sheets. In many African markets, imported roofing sheets are often sold by gauge but actual thickness may vary by 10â15%. For structural or load-bearing applications, specify thickness in millimetres and measure on delivery.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Sheet metal edges are razor-sharp. Always wear cut-resistant gloves when handling sheets, especially aluminium and stainless steel. Never use bare hands to guide sheet through a shear or brake. Use proper lifting techniquesâa 2m Ã 1m sheet of 2mm mild steel weighs approximately 31 kg and can cause serious back injury. Ensure adequate ventilation when welding galvanised or stainless steel, as the fumes are toxic. Store sheets vertically in racks to prevent falling and injury.

Corrosion and Material Protection

Corrosion is the electrochemical degradation of metal. In Africa, humidity, salt spray (coastal regions), and acid rain (industrial areas) accelerate corrosion. The three main protection methods are:

  • Barrier protection: Paint, powder coating, or plastic coating prevents moisture and oxygen from reaching the metal. Used on mild steel and aluminium.
  • Sacrificial protection: Galvanising (zinc coating) or zinc-rich paints. The zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel beneath.
  • Alloying: Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a passive oxide layer that self-heals when scratched (in the presence of oxygen).

For African conditions, galvanised steel is the minimum standard for roofing. In coastal areas within 10 km of the ocean, specify stainless steel 316 or aluminium for fasteners and flashings. Copper and aluminium should never be joined directlyâgalvanic corrosion will destroy the joint. Use isolating washers or transition fittings.

Material Selection for Specific Applications

Use this guide to select materials based on common African sheet metal applications:

  • Roofing (inland): Galvanised steel, 0.4â0.6 mm (26â24 gauge). Aluminium for premium jobs.
  • Roofing (coastal): Aluminium or stainless steel 316. Avoid bare mild steel.
  • Gutters and downspouts: Galvanised steel, aluminium, or copper (premium).
  • Kitchen equipment (food contact): Stainless steel 304, 0.8â1.2 mm (20â18 gauge).
  • Ducting and ventilation: Galvanised steel, 0.6â1.0 mm (24â20 gauge).
  • Vehicle body panels: Aluminium or mild steel (painted), 0.8â1.2 mm.
  • Decorative work: Copper, brass, or aluminium. Copper for high-end, aluminium for budget.
  • Signage: Aluminium, 1.5â3 mm, for outdoor durability.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the application: indoor/outdoor, coastal/inland, food contact/non-contact.
  2. Select the material family: ferrous (cheap, strong, needs protection) or non-ferrous (corrosion-resistant, lighter, more expensive).
  3. Specify thickness in millimetres, not just gauge. Verify with a caliper on delivery.
  4. Check ductility and malleability requirements for the forming process (bending, rolling, deep drawing).
  5. Confirm corrosion protection: galvanised, painted, or alloyed (stainless).
  6. Match tooling and cutting speeds to material hardnessâstainless requires slower speeds and sharp blades.
  7. Calculate material cost per square metre, including wastage and coating, before quoting the client.
  8. Store sheets vertically, off the ground, in a dry area to prevent rust and damage.

Further Reading

  • ASTM International â Standards for sheet metal thickness, testing, and material specifications (free abstracts).
  • ASM International â Materials property data and handbooks (free resources and previews).
  • ISO 9445:2002 â Continuously cold-rolled stainless steel narrow strip and cut lengths (free preview).
  • Copper Development Association â Free technical resources on copper sheet and roofing.
  • The Aluminum Association â Free design and fabrication guides for aluminium sheet.

Business tip: Keep a materials sample board in your workshop showing each sheet type, gauge, and coating. When a client questions your quote, show them the difference between a 0.4 mm galvanised sheet and a 0.6 mm aluminium sheet. Transparency builds trustâand repeat business.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a ferrous metal?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel contains iron, making it ferrous.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between ferrous and non-ferrous metals?
options: A) Ferrous metals are magnetic and contain iron
B) Non-ferrous metals are always stronger
quiz.explanation: Ferrous metals contain iron and are typically magnetic.

quiz.q: Which test can quickly identify a ferrous metal?
quiz.explanation: A magnet attracts ferrous metals, while most non-ferrous metals are not magnetic.

quiz.q: Which non-ferrous metal is commonly used for electrical wiring?
quiz.explanation: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity.

quiz.q: Why is mild steel often galvanized?
quiz.explanation: Galvanizing coats steel with zinc to protect it from corrosion.

quiz.q: What is the main alloying element in stainless steel that makes it corrosion-resistant?
quiz.explanation: Chromium forms a passive oxide layer that protects against rust.

quiz.q: Which metal is known for being lightweight and corrosion-resistant, often used for cooking pots?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum is light, conducts heat well, and resists corrosion.

quiz.q: What is brass an alloy of?
quiz.explanation: Brass is primarily copper and zinc.

quiz.q: Which property allows a metal to be stretched into wire without breaking?
quiz.explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires.

quiz.q: What does malleability refer to?
options: A) Ability to be hammered into thin sheets
quiz.explanation: Malleability is the ability to be deformed under compression, like hammering.

quiz.q: Which metal is more malleable: copper or steel?
quiz.explanation: Copper is highly malleable, while steel is less so.

quiz.q: How can you test the hardness of a metal?
options: B) Scratch it with a file
quiz.explanation: A file will bite into soft metal but slide on hard metal.

quiz.q: What does annealing do to a metal?
options: B) Makes it softer and more ductile
quiz.explanation: Annealing heats and cools metal to relieve stress and soften it.

quiz.q: In the gauge system, what does a higher gauge number mean?
quiz.explanation: Higher gauge numbers indicate thinner sheets.

quiz.q: Which tool is most precise for measuring sheet metal thickness?
quiz.explanation: A micrometer measures to 0.01 mm, more precise than a caliper.

quiz.q: What is the approximate thickness of 20 gauge mild steel in millimeters?
quiz.explanation: 20 gauge steel is about 0.9 mm thick.

quiz.q: Why is it important to specify the gauge standard when ordering metal?
options: A) Because gauge numbers differ for different metals
B) Because gauge is the same for all metals
quiz.explanation: Different standards (SWG, AWG) give different thicknesses for the same gauge number.

quiz.q: What is corrosion?
options: A) The gradual destruction of metal by chemical reaction
B) The process of welding metal
quiz.explanation: Corrosion is the deterioration of metal due to environmental reactions.

quiz.q: Which method protects steel by coating it with zinc?
quiz.explanation: Galvanizing applies a zinc coating that sacrificially protects the steel.

quiz.q: What is the green patina on copper?
quiz.explanation: The patina is a stable oxide layer that protects the copper beneath.

quiz.q: What is galvanic corrosion?
options: A) Corrosion of a single metal
B) Corrosion caused by two different metals in contact in a wet environment
quiz.explanation: When dissimilar metals touch in an electrolyte, one corrodes faster.

quiz.q: Which metal is best for a cooking pot that will be used with acidic foods?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel resists acid attack better than aluminum or copper.

quiz.q: For roofing in a coastal area with salt air, which material is most suitable?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum resists salt corrosion better than steel.

quiz.q: What is a common protective coating for outdoor steel structures in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Paint forms a barrier against moisture and oxygen.

quiz.q: Which property is most important for a metal that will be bent into complex shapes?
quiz.explanation: Ductility allows the metal to deform without cracking.

quiz.q: What does TIG welding require for aluminum?
options: A) A special gas and tungsten electrode
quiz.explanation: TIG welding uses tungsten and inert gas, suitable for aluminum.

quiz.q: Why is recycled car panel steel often used in African workshops?
options: A) It is cheap and available
quiz.explanation: Recycled mild steel from cars is affordable and widely available.

quiz.q: Which gauge is thicker: 16 or 20?
quiz.explanation: 16 gauge is thicker than 20 gauge.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of anodizing aluminum?
options: B) To improve corrosion resistance and allow dyeing
quiz.explanation: Anodizing thickens the oxide layer and can add color.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a method to protect steel from rust?
quiz.explanation: Annealing is a heat treatment to soften metal, not a protective coating.
